title: Prevent SQL Injection via Parameterized Queries
rule: Always use parameterized queries, prepared statements, or ORM bound variables when constructing database queries. Never concatenate untrusted user input directly into SQL strings. Ensure compliant design across all execution branches.
why_is_this_important: Unsanitized string concatenation in queries exposes the database to severe SQL injection vulnerabilities (CWE-89), potentially resulting in unauthorized data exfiltration or table destruction.
bad_example: db.Query('SELECT * FROM users WHERE email = ' + email)
good_example: db.Query('SELECT * FROM users WHERE email = $1', email)

examples.snippet: db.Query('SELECT * FROM users WHERE email = ' + email)
db.Query('SELECT * FROM users WHERE email = $1', email)

title: Mitigate Cross-Site Scripting (XSS) via Contextual Output Encoding
rule: Encode or sanitize all user-supplied content before rendering it into HTML, DOM attributes, or JavaScript execution contexts. Avoid raw innerHTML or unescaped template bindings. Ensure compliant design across all execution branches.
why_is_this_important: Unescaped user input rendered into the DOM enables attackers to execute arbitrary scripts in user sessions (CWE-79), compromising authentication tokens and private user data.

title: Enforce Cryptographically Secure Random Number Generation
rule: Use cryptographically secure pseudo-random number generators (CSPRNG) such as crypto/rand, secrets, or SecureRandom for generating tokens, session IDs, salt, and nonces. Never use default PRNGs. Ensure compliant design across all execution branches.
why_is_this_important: Standard pseudo-random generators (such as math/rand or Math.random) are deterministic and predictable, allowing attackers to anticipate generated tokens and bypass authentication.

title: Prevent Command Injection by Avoiding Shell Execution
rule: Invoke executables directly by passing arguments as discrete array elements rather than executing commands through an interactive shell (/bin/sh -c). Never interpolate untrusted strings into system commands. Ensure compliant design across all execution branches.
why_is_this_important: Shell command injection (CWE-78) allows remote adversaries to execute unauthorized operating system commands with the privileges of the application process.

title: Prevent Path Traversal by Validating and Sanitizing File Paths
rule: Resolve canonical file paths using secure path resolution APIs and verify that target paths remain strictly confined within an authorized root directory before performing file I/O operations. Ensure compliant design across all execution branches.
why_is_this_important: Path traversal vulnerabilities (CWE-22) allow attackers to access arbitrary files on the filesystem, including sensitive system configurations and credentials.
good_example: cleanPath := filepath.Clean(userInputPath); if !strings.HasPrefix(cleanPath, rootDir) { return ErrForbidden }

examples.snippet: cleanPath := filepath.Clean(userInputPath); if !strings.HasPrefix(cleanPath, rootDir) { return ErrForbidden }

title: Prohibit Deprecated and Broken Cryptographic Hash Algorithms
rule: Avoid legacy hashing algorithms such as MD5 and SHA-1 for digital signatures, password verification, or integrity validation. Mandate modern primitives like SHA-256, SHA-3, or BLAKE3. Ensure compliant design across all execution branches.
why_is_this_important: MD5 and SHA-1 suffer from proven practical collision attacks, rendering them unsuitable for security verification and digital signatures.

title: Enforce Password Hashing using Argon2id or Bcrypt
rule: Store user passwords using slow, memory-hard hashing algorithms such as Argon2id or Bcrypt with an appropriate cost factor. Never store plaintext, salted SHA-256, or fast hashes. Ensure compliant design across all execution branches.
why_is_this_important: Fast hash algorithms allow high-throughput GPU/ASIC offline dictionary attacks, exposing user credentials in the event of database exfiltration.

title: Avoid Hardcoded Cryptographic Keys and Shared Secrets
rule: Never embed symmetric encryption keys, HMAC secrets, or private certificates directly into source code. Inject them at runtime via secure environment managers or KMS envelopes. Ensure compliant design across all execution branches.
why_is_this_important: Hardcoded secrets in source code persist in version control history and decompiled binaries, leading to total compromise of cryptographic protections.

title: Verify Inbound Webhook Signatures using Constant-Time Comparison
rule: Always verify cryptographic HMAC signatures on incoming webhook payloads before parsing or processing. Use constant-time comparison algorithms to mitigate timing attacks. Ensure compliant design across all execution branches.
why_is_this_important: Accepting unverified webhook payloads allows malicious third parties to spoof events, manipulate balances, and trigger unauthorized automated actions.

title: Enforce Strict CORS Origin Whitelisting
rule: Configure Cross-Origin Resource Sharing (CORS) with an explicit whitelist of trusted origins. Never combine Access-Control-Allow-Origin: * with credentials enabled. Ensure compliant design across all execution branches.
why_is_this_important: Wildcard CORS combined with credentials allows malicious third-party websites to make authenticated cross-origin requests on behalf of logged-in users.

title: Prevent XML External Entity (XXE) Injection
rule: Disable external entity resolution (DTD) and entity expansion when parsing untrusted XML payloads in any parser or processor. Ensure compliant design across all execution branches.
why_is_this_important: XXE injection (CWE-611) allows attackers to read arbitrary server files, conduct internal port scans, or cause denial-of-service.

title: Prevent Server-Side Request Forgery (SSRF) on Outbound Requests
rule: Validate, sanitize, and restrict target destination URLs for outbound HTTP requests against an explicit domain allowlist and private IP filter (prevent access to RFC 1918 and link-local ranges). Ensure compliant design across all execution branches.
why_is_this_important: SSRF vulnerabilities (CWE-918) permit attackers to interact with internal cloud metadata services, VPC resources, and unauthenticated internal daemons.

title: Prevent Unbounded Goroutine or Thread Spawning
rule: Always dispatch asynchronous tasks through bounded worker pools or rate-limited semaphores. Never spawn bare goroutines or detached threads directly in request handlers. Ensure compliant design across all execution branches.
why_is_this_important: Unbounded thread/goroutine allocation under traffic spikes exhausts memory and scheduling resources, causing process crashes and denial of service.

title: Protect Concurrent Map Access with Mutual Exclusion
rule: Synchronize shared map reads and writes using sync.RWMutex, ConcurrentHashMap, or thread-safe sync.Map primitives. Ensure compliant design across all execution branches.
why_is_this_important: Concurrent unsynchronized reads and writes on native maps trigger fatal runtime panics and corrupt application state.

title: Mandate Resource Cleanup via Defer or Try-With-Resources
rule: Ensure all acquired I/O handles, file descriptors, database transactions, and network connections are guaranteed to be closed using defer, using/try-with-resources statements. Ensure compliant design across all execution branches.
why_is_this_important: Failing to close resources on early return or error paths leaks file descriptors and socket pools, eventually halting process I/O.
good_example: file, err := os.Open(filename); if err != nil { return err }; defer file.Close()

examples.snippet: file, err := os.Open(filename); if err != nil { return err }; defer file.Close()

title: Enforce Context Cancellation and Propagation Across Asynchronous Calls
rule: Propagate context.Context across all outbound RPCs, database queries, and async routines. Respect ctx.Done() to terminate in-flight work when requests are canceled. Ensure compliant design across all execution branches.
why_is_this_important: Ignoring context cancellation results in orphaned background computations, resource waste, and server memory starvation.

title: Avoid Deadlock Hazards by Establishing Deterministic Lock Ordering
rule: When acquiring multiple mutual exclusion locks simultaneously, always acquire and release them in a consistent, globally deterministic order across all call paths. Ensure compliant design across all execution branches.
why_is_this_important: Inconsistent lock ordering across concurrent threads creates circular wait conditions, precipitating catastrophic application deadlocks.
bad_example: muB.Lock(); muA.Lock(); defer muA.Unlock(); defer muB.Unlock()
good_example: muA.Lock(); muB.Lock(); defer muB.Unlock(); defer muA.Unlock()

examples.snippet: muB.Lock(); muA.Lock(); defer muA.Unlock(); defer muB.Unlock()
muA.Lock(); muB.Lock(); defer muB.Unlock(); defer muA.Unlock()

title: Avoid Double-Closing Channels in Go
rule: Ensure a channel is only closed by the single designated sender goroutine that owns it. Never close a channel from multiple concurrent receiver routines. Ensure compliant design across all execution branches.
why_is_this_important: Closing an already closed channel causes an immediate, non-recoverable runtime panic in Go.

title: Prevent Unbuffered Channel Leaks on Early Exit
rule: Ensure sending to an unbuffered channel cannot block indefinitely if the receiving goroutine exits early due to errors or timeouts. Ensure compliant design across all execution branches.
why_is_this_important: Blocked goroutines waiting to send on unbuffered channels remain pinned in memory indefinitely, causing silent goroutine leaks.
bad_example: ch := make(chan int); go func() { ch <- compute() }()
good_example: ch := make(chan int, 1); go func() { ch <- compute() }(); return <-ch

examples.snippet: ch := make(chan int); go func() { ch <- compute() }()
ch := make(chan int, 1); go func() { ch <- compute() }(); return <-ch

title: Eliminate N+1 Query Antipattern in Data Fetching
rule: Eagerly load related relational records using batch queries (IN clauses, JOINs, or DataLoader patterns) instead of issuing individual queries inside iteration loops. Ensure compliant design across all execution branches.
why_is_this_important: Executing individual database round-trips inside loops causes significant query latency and database connection exhaustion under scale.

title: Enforce Pagination and Result Limits on Collection Endpoints
rule: Always enforce mandatory pagination limits (e.g. limit and offset or cursor tokens) on database queries returning collections. Never perform unbounded SELECT operations. Ensure compliant design across all execution branches.
why_is_this_important: Unbounded database queries can pull hundreds of thousands of records into memory, triggering out-of-memory crashes and saturating database I/O.
good_example: db.Query('SELECT * FROM audit_logs ORDER BY created_at DESC LIMIT $1 OFFSET $2', limit, offset)

examples.snippet: db.Query('SELECT * FROM audit_logs ORDER BY created_at DESC LIMIT $1 OFFSET $2', limit, offset)

title: Ensure Database Transactions Always Execute Rollback on Failure
rule: Always wrap database transaction scopes with deferred rollback guards to ensure failed operations clean up transaction locks and prevent dangling transactions. Ensure compliant design across all execution branches.
why_is_this_important: Uncommitted transactions left open due to early returns or runtime errors hold database locks and deplete transaction slots.
good_example: tx, err := db.Begin(); if err != nil { return err }; defer tx.Rollback(); doWork(tx); return tx.Commit()

examples.snippet: tx, err := db.Begin(); if err != nil { return err }; defer tx.Rollback(); doWork(tx); return tx.Commit()

title: Avoid Index Suppression by Applying Functions to Filter Columns
rule: Do not wrap indexed database columns in scalar functions within WHERE clauses (e.g., LOWER(email) or DATE(created_at)). Use functional indexes or range bounds instead. Ensure compliant design across all execution branches.
why_is_this_important: Applying functions to indexed columns invalidates index lookups, forcing the database engine to perform expensive full table scans.

title: Prohibit Swallowing Errors Without Logging or Propagation
rule: Always handle or propagate errors returned from fallible operations. Never discard errors with blank identifiers or empty catch blocks without explicit justification. Ensure compliant design across all execution branches.
why_is_this_important: Swallowing errors hides failures, causes silent state corruption, and turns production defects into impossible-to-diagnose phantom bugs.
good_example: data, err := os.ReadFile(path); if err != nil { return fmt.Errorf('read config: %w', err) }

examples.snippet: data, err := os.ReadFile(path); if err != nil { return fmt.Errorf('read config: %w', err) }

title: Enforce Structured Logging with Key-Value Context
rule: Emit log statements with structured key-value attributes (e.g., slog, zap, winston) rather than unparsed string formatting. Include correlation IDs and tenant identifiers. Ensure compliant design across all execution branches.
why_is_this_important: Unstructured string logs cannot be indexed, queried, or alerted upon reliably by modern log management platforms like Datadog, ELK, or OpenTelemetry.

title: Avoid Logging Sensitive Credentials or PII
rule: Sanitize and redact authorization headers, passwords, session tokens, social security numbers, and payment details before emitting log entries. Ensure compliant design across all execution branches.
why_is_this_important: Sensitive data in log streams frequently ends up in monitoring dashboards, third-party log providers, and developer laptops, violating privacy regulations.

title: Wrap Errors with Domain Context Rather Than Raw String Errors
rule: Wrap errors using standard formatters (%w in Go, custom error hierarchies in TypeScript/Python) to preserve underlying error causes while adding operation context. Ensure compliant design across all execution branches.
why_is_this_important: Returning bare error strings destroys stack traces and root cause inspectability, hindering effective automated error handling.

title: Enforce Proper HTTP Status Code Semantics
rule: Return semantically appropriate HTTP status codes (200 for OK, 201 for Created, 400 for Client Error, 401 for Unauthenticated, 403 for Forbidden, 404 for Not Found). Never return 200 with an error payload. Ensure compliant design across all execution branches.
why_is_this_important: Returning HTTP 200 with embedded error flags breaks HTTP caching layers, API gateways, monitoring alerts, and client retry logic.

title: Implement Distributed Idempotency on State-Mutating Endpoints
rule: Ensure billing, payment, and critical resource creation endpoints require and enforce unique idempotency keys to prevent duplicate execution on network retries. Ensure compliant design across all execution branches.
why_is_this_important: Transient network retries without idempotency keys lead to double charges, duplicate records, and inconsistent external system states.
good_example: func CreatePayment(w http.ResponseWriter, r *http.Request) { key := r.Header.Get('Idempotency-Key'); dedupeAndExecute(key) }

examples.snippet: func CreatePayment(w http.ResponseWriter, r *http.Request) { key := r.Header.Get('Idempotency-Key'); dedupeAndExecute(key) }

title: Maintain API Versioning and Prevent Breaking Changes
rule: Introduce new API fields as optional additions and maintain existing endpoint schemas under versioned prefixes (/v1, /v2) to ensure backward compatibility for mobile and third-party clients. Ensure compliant design across all execution branches.
why_is_this_important: Renaming or removing fields in unversioned API contracts instantly crashes older mobile app releases and third-party integrations.

why_is_this_important: Path traversal vulnerabilities (CWE-22) allow attackers to access arbitrary files on the filesystem, including sensitive system configurations and credentials.
good_example: cleanPath := filepath.Clean(userInputPath); if !strings.HasPrefix(cleanPath, rootDir) { return ErrForbidden }

examples.snippet: cleanPath := filepath.Clean(userInputPath); if !strings.HasPrefix(cleanPath, rootDir) { return ErrForbidden }

title: Prohibit Deprecated and Broken Cryptographic Hash Algorithms (Standard Policy #3)
rule: Avoid legacy hashing algorithms such as MD5 and SHA-1 for digital signatures, password verification, or integrity validation. Mandate modern primitives like SHA-256, SHA-3, or BLAKE3. Ensure compliant design across all execution branches.
why_is_this_important: MD5 and SHA-1 suffer from proven practical collision attacks, rendering them unsuitable for security verification and digital signatures.

title: Enforce Password Hashing using Argon2id or Bcrypt (Standard Policy #3)
rule: Store user passwords using slow, memory-hard hashing algorithms such as Argon2id or Bcrypt with an appropriate cost factor. Never store plaintext, salted SHA-256, or fast hashes. Ensure compliant design across all execution branches.
why_is_this_important: Fast hash algorithms allow high-throughput GPU/ASIC offline dictionary attacks, exposing user credentials in the event of database exfiltration.

title: Avoid Hardcoded Cryptographic Keys and Shared Secrets (Standard Policy #3)
rule: Never embed symmetric encryption keys, HMAC secrets, or private certificates directly into source code. Inject them at runtime via secure environment managers or KMS envelopes. Ensure compliant design across all execution branches.
why_is_this_important: Hardcoded secrets in source code persist in version control history and decompiled binaries, leading to total compromise of cryptographic protections.

title: Verify Inbound Webhook Signatures using Constant-Time Comparison (Standard Policy #3)
rule: Always verify cryptographic HMAC signatures on incoming webhook payloads before parsing or processing. Use constant-time comparison algorithms to mitigate timing attacks. Ensure compliant design across all execution branches.
why_is_this_important: Accepting unverified webhook payloads allows malicious third parties to spoof events, manipulate balances, and trigger unauthorized automated actions.

title: Enforce Strict CORS Origin Whitelisting (Standard Policy #3)
rule: Configure Cross-Origin Resource Sharing (CORS) with an explicit whitelist of trusted origins. Never combine Access-Control-Allow-Origin: * with credentials enabled. Ensure compliant design across all execution branches.
why_is_this_important: Wildcard CORS combined with credentials allows malicious third-party websites to make authenticated cross-origin requests on behalf of logged-in users.

title: Prevent XML External Entity (XXE) Injection (Standard Policy #3)
rule: Disable external entity resolution (DTD) and entity expansion when parsing untrusted XML payloads in any parser or processor. Ensure compliant design across all execution branches.
why_is_this_important: XXE injection (CWE-611) allows attackers to read arbitrary server files, conduct internal port scans, or cause denial-of-service.

title: Prevent Server-Side Request Forgery (SSRF) on Outbound Requests (Standard Policy #3)
rule: Validate, sanitize, and restrict target destination URLs for outbound HTTP requests against an explicit domain allowlist and private IP filter (prevent access to RFC 1918 and link-local ranges). Ensure compliant design across all execution branches.
why_is_this_important: SSRF vulnerabilities (CWE-918) permit attackers to interact with internal cloud metadata services, VPC resources, and unauthenticated internal daemons.

title: Prevent Unbounded Goroutine or Thread Spawning (Standard Policy #3)
rule: Always dispatch asynchronous tasks through bounded worker pools or rate-limited semaphores. Never spawn bare goroutines or detached threads directly in request handlers. Ensure compliant design across all execution branches.
why_is_this_important: Unbounded thread/goroutine allocation under traffic spikes exhausts memory and scheduling resources, causing process crashes and denial of service.

title: Protect Concurrent Map Access with Mutual Exclusion (Standard Policy #3)
rule: Synchronize shared map reads and writes using sync.RWMutex, ConcurrentHashMap, or thread-safe sync.Map primitives. Ensure compliant design across all execution branches.
why_is_this_important: Concurrent unsynchronized reads and writes on native maps trigger fatal runtime panics and corrupt application state.

title: Mandate Resource Cleanup via Defer or Try-With-Resources (Standard Policy #3)
rule: Ensure all acquired I/O handles, file descriptors, database transactions, and network connections are guaranteed to be closed using defer, using/try-with-resources statements. Ensure compliant design across all execution branches.
why_is_this_important: Failing to close resources on early return or error paths leaks file descriptors and socket pools, eventually halting process I/O.
good_example: file, err := os.Open(filename); if err != nil { return err }; defer file.Close()

examples.snippet: file, err := os.Open(filename); if err != nil { return err }; defer file.Close()

title: Enforce Context Cancellation and Propagation Across Asynchronous Calls (Standard Policy #4)
rule: Propagate context.Context across all outbound RPCs, database queries, and async routines. Respect ctx.Done() to terminate in-flight work when requests are canceled. Ensure compliant design across all execution branches.
why_is_this_important: Ignoring context cancellation results in orphaned background computations, resource waste, and server memory starvation.

title: Avoid Deadlock Hazards by Establishing Deterministic Lock Ordering (Standard Policy #4)
rule: When acquiring multiple mutual exclusion locks simultaneously, always acquire and release them in a consistent, globally deterministic order across all call paths. Ensure compliant design across all execution branches.
why_is_this_important: Inconsistent lock ordering across concurrent threads creates circular wait conditions, precipitating catastrophic application deadlocks.
bad_example: muB.Lock(); muA.Lock(); defer muA.Unlock(); defer muB.Unlock()
good_example: muA.Lock(); muB.Lock(); defer muB.Unlock(); defer muA.Unlock()

examples.snippet: muB.Lock(); muA.Lock(); defer muA.Unlock(); defer muB.Unlock()
muA.Lock(); muB.Lock(); defer muB.Unlock(); defer muA.Unlock()

title: Avoid Double-Closing Channels in Go (Standard Policy #4)
rule: Ensure a channel is only closed by the single designated sender goroutine that owns it. Never close a channel from multiple concurrent receiver routines. Ensure compliant design across all execution branches.
why_is_this_important: Closing an already closed channel causes an immediate, non-recoverable runtime panic in Go.

title: Prevent Unbuffered Channel Leaks on Early Exit (Standard Policy #4)
rule: Ensure sending to an unbuffered channel cannot block indefinitely if the receiving goroutine exits early due to errors or timeouts. Ensure compliant design across all execution branches.
why_is_this_important: Blocked goroutines waiting to send on unbuffered channels remain pinned in memory indefinitely, causing silent goroutine leaks.
bad_example: ch := make(chan int); go func() { ch <- compute() }()
good_example: ch := make(chan int, 1); go func() { ch <- compute() }(); return <-ch

examples.snippet: ch := make(chan int); go func() { ch <- compute() }()
ch := make(chan int, 1); go func() { ch <- compute() }(); return <-ch

title: Eliminate N+1 Query Antipattern in Data Fetching (Standard Policy #4)
rule: Eagerly load related relational records using batch queries (IN clauses, JOINs, or DataLoader patterns) instead of issuing individual queries inside iteration loops. Ensure compliant design across all execution branches.
why_is_this_important: Executing individual database round-trips inside loops causes significant query latency and database connection exhaustion under scale.

title: Enforce Pagination and Result Limits on Collection Endpoints (Standard Policy #4)
rule: Always enforce mandatory pagination limits (e.g. limit and offset or cursor tokens) on database queries returning collections. Never perform unbounded SELECT operations. Ensure compliant design across all execution branches.
why_is_this_important: Unbounded database queries can pull hundreds of thousands of records into memory, triggering out-of-memory crashes and saturating database I/O.
good_example: db.Query('SELECT * FROM audit_logs ORDER BY created_at DESC LIMIT $1 OFFSET $2', limit, offset)

examples.snippet: db.Query('SELECT * FROM audit_logs ORDER BY created_at DESC LIMIT $1 OFFSET $2', limit, offset)

title: Ensure Database Transactions Always Execute Rollback on Failure (Standard Policy #4)
rule: Always wrap database transaction scopes with deferred rollback guards to ensure failed operations clean up transaction locks and prevent dangling transactions. Ensure compliant design across all execution branches.
why_is_this_important: Uncommitted transactions left open due to early returns or runtime errors hold database locks and deplete transaction slots.
good_example: tx, err := db.Begin(); if err != nil { return err }; defer tx.Rollback(); doWork(tx); return tx.Commit()

examples.snippet: tx, err := db.Begin(); if err != nil { return err }; defer tx.Rollback(); doWork(tx); return tx.Commit()

title: Avoid Index Suppression by Applying Functions to Filter Columns (Standard Policy #4)
rule: Do not wrap indexed database columns in scalar functions within WHERE clauses (e.g., LOWER(email) or DATE(created_at)). Use functional indexes or range bounds instead. Ensure compliant design across all execution branches.
why_is_this_important: Applying functions to indexed columns invalidates index lookups, forcing the database engine to perform expensive full table scans.

title: Prohibit Swallowing Errors Without Logging or Propagation (Standard Policy #4)
rule: Always handle or propagate errors returned from fallible operations. Never discard errors with blank identifiers or empty catch blocks without explicit justification. Ensure compliant design across all execution branches.
why_is_this_important: Swallowing errors hides failures, causes silent state corruption, and turns production defects into impossible-to-diagnose phantom bugs.
good_example: data, err := os.ReadFile(path); if err != nil { return fmt.Errorf('read config: %w', err) }

examples.snippet: data, err := os.ReadFile(path); if err != nil { return fmt.Errorf('read config: %w', err) }

title: Enforce Structured Logging with Key-Value Context (Standard Policy #4)
rule: Emit log statements with structured key-value attributes (e.g., slog, zap, winston) rather than unparsed string formatting. Include correlation IDs and tenant identifiers. Ensure compliant design across all execution branches.
why_is_this_important: Unstructured string logs cannot be indexed, queried, or alerted upon reliably by modern log management platforms like Datadog, ELK, or OpenTelemetry.

title: Avoid Logging Sensitive Credentials or PII (Standard Policy #4)
rule: Sanitize and redact authorization headers, passwords, session tokens, social security numbers, and payment details before emitting log entries. Ensure compliant design across all execution branches.
why_is_this_important: Sensitive data in log streams frequently ends up in monitoring dashboards, third-party log providers, and developer laptops, violating privacy regulations.

title: Wrap Errors with Domain Context Rather Than Raw String Errors (Standard Policy #4)
rule: Wrap errors using standard formatters (%w in Go, custom error hierarchies in TypeScript/Python) to preserve underlying error causes while adding operation context. Ensure compliant design across all execution branches.
why_is_this_important: Returning bare error strings destroys stack traces and root cause inspectability, hindering effective automated error handling.

title: Enforce Proper HTTP Status Code Semantics (Standard Policy #4)
rule: Return semantically appropriate HTTP status codes (200 for OK, 201 for Created, 400 for Client Error, 401 for Unauthenticated, 403 for Forbidden, 404 for Not Found). Never return 200 with an error payload. Ensure compliant design across all execution branches.
why_is_this_important: Returning HTTP 200 with embedded error flags breaks HTTP caching layers, API gateways, monitoring alerts, and client retry logic.

title: Implement Distributed Idempotency on State-Mutating Endpoints (Standard Policy #4)
rule: Ensure billing, payment, and critical resource creation endpoints require and enforce unique idempotency keys to prevent duplicate execution on network retries. Ensure compliant design across all execution branches.
why_is_this_important: Transient network retries without idempotency keys lead to double charges, duplicate records, and inconsistent external system states.
good_example: func CreatePayment(w http.ResponseWriter, r *http.Request) { key := r.Header.Get('Idempotency-Key'); dedupeAndExecute(key) }

examples.snippet: func CreatePayment(w http.ResponseWriter, r *http.Request) { key := r.Header.Get('Idempotency-Key'); dedupeAndExecute(key) }

title: Maintain API Versioning and Prevent Breaking Changes (Standard Policy #4)
rule: Introduce new API fields as optional additions and maintain existing endpoint schemas under versioned prefixes (/v1, /v2) to ensure backward compatibility for mobile and third-party clients. Ensure compliant design across all execution branches.
why_is_this_important: Renaming or removing fields in unversioned API contracts instantly crashes older mobile app releases and third-party integrations.

title: Prevent SQL Injection via Parameterized Queries (Standard Policy #4)
rule: Always use parameterized queries, prepared statements, or ORM bound variables when constructing database queries. Never concatenate untrusted user input directly into SQL strings. Ensure compliant design across all execution branches.
why_is_this_important: Unsanitized string concatenation in queries exposes the database to severe SQL injection vulnerabilities (CWE-89), potentially resulting in unauthorized data exfiltration or table destruction.
bad_example: db.Query('SELECT * FROM users WHERE email = ' + email)
good_example: db.Query('SELECT * FROM users WHERE email = $1', email)

examples.snippet: db.Query('SELECT * FROM users WHERE email = ' + email)
db.Query('SELECT * FROM users WHERE email = $1', email)

title: Mitigate Cross-Site Scripting (XSS) via Contextual Output Encoding (Standard Policy #4)
rule: Encode or sanitize all user-supplied content before rendering it into HTML, DOM attributes, or JavaScript execution contexts. Avoid raw innerHTML or unescaped template bindings. Ensure compliant design across all execution branches.
why_is_this_important: Unescaped user input rendered into the DOM enables attackers to execute arbitrary scripts in user sessions (CWE-79), compromising authentication tokens and private user data.

title: Enforce Cryptographically Secure Random Number Generation (Standard Policy #4)

why_is_this_important: Standard pseudo-random generators (such as math/rand or Math.random) are deterministic and predictable, allowing attackers to anticipate generated tokens and bypass authentication.

why_is_this_important: Shell command injection (CWE-78) allows remote adversaries to execute unauthorized operating system commands with the privileges of the application process.

title: Verify Inbound Webhook Signatures using Constant-Time Comparison (Standard Policy #6)

title: Enforce Strict CORS Origin Whitelisting (Standard Policy #6)
rule: Configure Cross-Origin Resource Sharing (CORS) with an explicit whitelist of trusted origins. Never combine Access-Control-Allow-Origin: * with credentials enabled. Ensure compliant design across all execution branches.
why_is_this_important: Wildcard CORS combined with credentials allows malicious third-party websites to make authenticated cross-origin requests on behalf of logged-in users.

title: Prevent XML External Entity (XXE) Injection (Standard Policy #6)
rule: Disable external entity resolution (DTD) and entity expansion when parsing untrusted XML payloads in any parser or processor. Ensure compliant design across all execution branches.
why_is_this_important: XXE injection (CWE-611) allows attackers to read arbitrary server files, conduct internal port scans, or cause denial-of-service.

title: Prevent Server-Side Request Forgery (SSRF) on Outbound Requests (Standard Policy #6)
rule: Validate, sanitize, and restrict target destination URLs for outbound HTTP requests against an explicit domain allowlist and private IP filter (prevent access to RFC 1918 and link-local ranges). Ensure compliant design across all execution branches.
why_is_this_important: SSRF vulnerabilities (CWE-918) permit attackers to interact with internal cloud metadata services, VPC resources, and unauthenticated internal daemons.

title: Prevent Unbounded Goroutine or Thread Spawning (Standard Policy #6)
rule: Always dispatch asynchronous tasks through bounded worker pools or rate-limited semaphores. Never spawn bare goroutines or detached threads directly in request handlers. Ensure compliant design across all execution branches.
why_is_this_important: Unbounded thread/goroutine allocation under traffic spikes exhausts memory and scheduling resources, causing process crashes and denial of service.

title: Protect Concurrent Map Access with Mutual Exclusion (Standard Policy #6)
rule: Synchronize shared map reads and writes using sync.RWMutex, ConcurrentHashMap, or thread-safe sync.Map primitives. Ensure compliant design across all execution branches.

title: Prevent Server-Side Request Forgery (SSRF) on Outbound Requests (Standard Policy #8)

why_is_this_important: SSRF vulnerabilities (CWE-918) permit attackers to interact with internal cloud metadata services, VPC resources, and unauthenticated internal daemons.

title: Prevent Unbounded Goroutine or Thread Spawning (Standard Policy #8)
rule: Always dispatch asynchronous tasks through bounded worker pools or rate-limited semaphores. Never spawn bare goroutines or detached threads directly in request handlers. Ensure compliant design across all execution branches.
why_is_this_important: Unbounded thread/goroutine allocation under traffic spikes exhausts memory and scheduling resources, causing process crashes and denial of service.

title: Protect Concurrent Map Access with Mutual Exclusion (Standard Policy #8)
rule: Synchronize shared map reads and writes using sync.RWMutex, ConcurrentHashMap, or thread-safe sync.Map primitives. Ensure compliant design across all execution branches.
why_is_this_important: Concurrent unsynchronized reads and writes on native maps trigger fatal runtime panics and corrupt application state.

title: Mandate Resource Cleanup via Defer or Try-With-Resources (Standard Policy #8)
rule: Ensure all acquired I/O handles, file descriptors, database transactions, and network connections are guaranteed to be closed using defer, using/try-with-resources statements. Ensure compliant design across all execution branches.
why_is_this_important: Failing to close resources on early return or error paths leaks file descriptors and socket pools, eventually halting process I/O.

title: Enforce Context Cancellation and Propagation Across Asynchronous Calls (Standard Policy #8)
rule: Propagate context.Context across all outbound RPCs, database queries, and async routines. Respect ctx.Done() to terminate in-flight work when requests are canceled. Ensure compliant design across all execution branches.
why_is_this_important: Ignoring context cancellation results in orphaned background computations, resource waste, and server memory starvation.

title: Avoid Deadlock Hazards by Establishing Deterministic Lock Ordering (Standard Policy #8)
rule: When acquiring multiple mutual exclusion locks simultaneously, always acquire and release them in a consistent, globally deterministic order across all call paths. Ensure compliant design across all execution branches.

title: Avoid Double-Closing Channels in Go (Standard Policy #8)

why_is_this_important: Closing an already closed channel causes an immediate, non-recoverable runtime panic in Go.

title: Prevent Unbuffered Channel Leaks on Early Exit (Standard Policy #8)

title: Enforce Pagination and Result Limits on Collection Endpoints (Standard Policy #9)

title: Avoid Index Suppression by Applying Functions to Filter Columns (Standard Policy #9)

title: Prohibit Swallowing Errors Without Logging or Propagation (Standard Policy #9)

title: Enforce Structured Logging with Key-Value Context (Standard Policy #9)

title: Avoid Logging Sensitive Credentials or PII (Standard Policy #9)

title: Wrap Errors with Domain Context Rather Than Raw String Errors (Standard Policy #9)
rule: Wrap errors using standard formatters (%w in Go, custom error hierarchies in TypeScript/Python) to preserve underlying error causes while adding operation context. Ensure compliant design across all execution branches.
why_is_this_important: Returning bare error strings destroys stack traces and root cause inspectability, hindering effective automated error handling.

title: Enforce Proper HTTP Status Code Semantics (Standard Policy #9)
rule: Return semantically appropriate HTTP status codes (200 for OK, 201 for Created, 400 for Client Error, 401 for Unauthenticated, 403 for Forbidden, 404 for Not Found). Never return 200 with an error payload. Ensure compliant design across all execution branches.
why_is_this_important: Returning HTTP 200 with embedded error flags breaks HTTP caching layers, API gateways, monitoring alerts, and client retry logic.

title: Implement Distributed Idempotency on State-Mutating Endpoints (Standard Policy #9)

title: Avoid Logging Sensitive Credentials or PII (Standard Policy #11)

title: Prevent Unbuffered Channel Leaks on Early Exit (Standard Policy #13)

title: Enforce Pagination and Result Limits on Collection Endpoints (Standard Policy #13)

title: Prohibit Swallowing Errors Without Logging or Propagation (Standard Policy #13)

title: Enforce Structured Logging with Key-Value Context (Standard Policy #13)

title: Avoid Logging Sensitive Credentials or PII (Standard Policy #14)

title: Wrap Errors with Domain Context Rather Than Raw String Errors (Standard Policy #14)
rule: Wrap errors using standard formatters (%w in Go, custom error hierarchies in TypeScript/Python) to preserve underlying error causes while adding operation context. Ensure compliant design across all execution branches.
why_is_this_important: Returning bare error strings destroys stack traces and root cause inspectability, hindering effective automated error handling.

title: Enforce Proper HTTP Status Code Semantics (Standard Policy #14)
rule: Return semantically appropriate HTTP status codes (200 for OK, 201 for Created, 400 for Client Error, 401 for Unauthenticated, 403 for Forbidden, 404 for Not Found). Never return 200 with an error payload. Ensure compliant design across all execution branches.
why_is_this_important: Returning HTTP 200 with embedded error flags breaks HTTP caching layers, API gateways, monitoring alerts, and client retry logic.

title: Implement Distributed Idempotency on State-Mutating Endpoints (Standard Policy #14)

title: Enforce Cryptographically Secure Random Number Generation (Standard Policy #14)

why_is_this_important: Standard pseudo-random generators (such as math/rand or Math.random) are deterministic and predictable, allowing attackers to anticipate generated tokens and bypass authentication.

title: Prevent Command Injection by Avoiding Shell Execution (Standard Policy #14)

why_is_this_important: Shell command injection (CWE-78) allows remote adversaries to execute unauthorized operating system commands with the privileges of the application process.

title: Prevent Path Traversal by Validating and Sanitizing File Paths (Standard Policy #14)

title: Prohibit Deprecated and Broken Cryptographic Hash Algorithms (Standard Policy #14)
rule: Avoid legacy hashing algorithms such as MD5 and SHA-1 for digital signatures, password verification, or integrity validation. Mandate modern primitives like SHA-256, SHA-3, or BLAKE3. Ensure compliant design across all execution branches.
why_is_this_important: MD5 and SHA-1 suffer from proven practical collision attacks, rendering them unsuitable for security verification and digital signatures.

title: Enforce Password Hashing using Argon2id or Bcrypt (Standard Policy #14)

title: Avoid Hardcoded Cryptographic Keys and Shared Secrets (Standard Policy #14)

why_is_this_important: Hardcoded secrets in source code persist in version control history and decompiled binaries, leading to total compromise of cryptographic protections.

title: Verify Inbound Webhook Signatures using Constant-Time Comparison (Standard Policy #14)

title: Enforce Strict CORS Origin Whitelisting (Standard Policy #14)

why_is_this_important: Wildcard CORS combined with credentials allows malicious third-party websites to make authenticated cross-origin requests on behalf of logged-in users.

title: Enforce Pagination and Result Limits on Collection Endpoints (Standard Policy #16)

title: Prohibit Swallowing Errors Without Logging or Propagation (Standard Policy #18)

title: Enforce Structured Logging with Key-Value Context (Standard Policy #18)
rule: Emit log statements with structured key-value attributes (e.g., slog, zap, winston) rather than unparsed string formatting. Include correlation IDs and tenant identifiers. Ensure compliant design across all execution branches.
why_is_this_important: Unstructured string logs cannot be indexed, queried, or alerted upon reliably by modern log management platforms like Datadog, ELK, or OpenTelemetry.

title: Avoid Logging Sensitive Credentials or PII (Standard Policy #18)
rule: Sanitize and redact authorization headers, passwords, session tokens, social security numbers, and payment details before emitting log entries. Ensure compliant design across all execution branches.
why_is_this_important: Sensitive data in log streams frequently ends up in monitoring dashboards, third-party log providers, and developer laptops, violating privacy regulations.

title: Wrap Errors with Domain Context Rather Than Raw String Errors (Standard Policy #18)
rule: Wrap errors using standard formatters (%w in Go, custom error hierarchies in TypeScript/Python) to preserve underlying error causes while adding operation context. Ensure compliant design across all execution branches.
why_is_this_important: Returning bare error strings destroys stack traces and root cause inspectability, hindering effective automated error handling.

title: Enforce Proper HTTP Status Code Semantics (Standard Policy #18)
rule: Return semantically appropriate HTTP status codes (200 for OK, 201 for Created, 400 for Client Error, 401 for Unauthenticated, 403 for Forbidden, 404 for Not Found). Never return 200 with an error payload. Ensure compliant design across all execution branches.
why_is_this_important: Returning HTTP 200 with embedded error flags breaks HTTP caching layers, API gateways, monitoring alerts, and client retry logic.

title: Implement Distributed Idempotency on State-Mutating Endpoints (Standard Policy #18)

title: Prevent Path Traversal by Validating and Sanitizing File Paths (Standard Policy #19)

rule: Emit log statements with structured key-value attributes (e.g., slog, zap, winston) rather than unparsed string formatting. Include correlation IDs and tenant identifiers. Ensure compliant design across all execution branches.
why_is_this_important: Unstructured string logs cannot be indexed, queried, or alerted upon reliably by modern log management platforms like Datadog, ELK, or OpenTelemetry.

title: Avoid Logging Sensitive Credentials or PII (Standard Policy #21)
rule: Sanitize and redact authorization headers, passwords, session tokens, social security numbers, and payment details before emitting log entries. Ensure compliant design across all execution branches.
why_is_this_important: Sensitive data in log streams frequently ends up in monitoring dashboards, third-party log providers, and developer laptops, violating privacy regulations.

title: Wrap Errors with Domain Context Rather Than Raw String Errors (Standard Policy #21)
rule: Wrap errors using standard formatters (%w in Go, custom error hierarchies in TypeScript/Python) to preserve underlying error causes while adding operation context. Ensure compliant design across all execution branches.
why_is_this_important: Returning bare error strings destroys stack traces and root cause inspectability, hindering effective automated error handling.

title: Enforce Proper HTTP Status Code Semantics (Standard Policy #21)
rule: Return semantically appropriate HTTP status codes (200 for OK, 201 for Created, 400 for Client Error, 401 for Unauthenticated, 403 for Forbidden, 404 for Not Found). Never return 200 with an error payload. Ensure compliant design across all execution branches.
why_is_this_important: Returning HTTP 200 with embedded error flags breaks HTTP caching layers, API gateways, monitoring alerts, and client retry logic.

title: Implement Distributed Idempotency on State-Mutating Endpoints (Standard Policy #21)
rule: Ensure billing, payment, and critical resource creation endpoints require and enforce unique idempotency keys to prevent duplicate execution on network retries. Ensure compliant design across all execution branches.
why_is_this_important: Transient network retries without idempotency keys lead to double charges, duplicate records, and inconsistent external system states.

title: Maintain API Versioning and Prevent Breaking Changes (Standard Policy #21)

title: Prevent SQL Injection via Parameterized Queries (Standard Policy #21)

title: Enforce Cryptographically Secure Random Number Generation (Standard Policy #21)

title: Prevent Unbounded Goroutine or Thread Spawning (Standard Policy #21)

why_is_this_important: Returning HTTP 200 with embedded error flags breaks HTTP caching layers, API gateways, monitoring alerts, and client retry logic.

title: Implement Distributed Idempotency on State-Mutating Endpoints (Standard Policy #23)
rule: Ensure billing, payment, and critical resource creation endpoints require and enforce unique idempotency keys to prevent duplicate execution on network retries. Ensure compliant design across all execution branches.
why_is_this_important: Transient network retries without idempotency keys lead to double charges, duplicate records, and inconsistent external system states.
good_example: func CreatePayment(w http.ResponseWriter, r *http.Request) { key := r.Header.Get('Idempotency-Key'); dedupeAndExecute(key) }

examples.snippet: func CreatePayment(w http.ResponseWriter, r *http.Request) { key := r.Header.Get('Idempotency-Key'); dedupeAndExecute(key) }

title: Maintain API Versioning and Prevent Breaking Changes (Standard Policy #23)
rule: Introduce new API fields as optional additions and maintain existing endpoint schemas under versioned prefixes (/v1, /v2) to ensure backward compatibility for mobile and third-party clients. Ensure compliant design across all execution branches.
why_is_this_important: Renaming or removing fields in unversioned API contracts instantly crashes older mobile app releases and third-party integrations.

title: Prevent SQL Injection via Parameterized Queries (Standard Policy #23)
rule: Always use parameterized queries, prepared statements, or ORM bound variables when constructing database queries. Never concatenate untrusted user input directly into SQL strings. Ensure compliant design across all execution branches.
why_is_this_important: Unsanitized string concatenation in queries exposes the database to severe SQL injection vulnerabilities (CWE-89), potentially resulting in unauthorized data exfiltration or table destruction.
bad_example: db.Query('SELECT * FROM users WHERE email = ' + email)
good_example: db.Query('SELECT * FROM users WHERE email = $1', email)

examples.snippet: db.Query('SELECT * FROM users WHERE email = ' + email)
db.Query('SELECT * FROM users WHERE email = $1', email)

title: Mitigate Cross-Site Scripting (XSS) via Contextual Output Encoding (Standard Policy #23)
rule: Encode or sanitize all user-supplied content before rendering it into HTML, DOM attributes, or JavaScript execution contexts. Avoid raw innerHTML or unescaped template bindings. Ensure compliant design across all execution branches.
why_is_this_important: Unescaped user input rendered into the DOM enables attackers to execute arbitrary scripts in user sessions (CWE-79), compromising authentication tokens and private user data.

title: Enforce Cryptographically Secure Random Number Generation (Standard Policy #23)
rule: Use cryptographically secure pseudo-random number generators (CSPRNG) such as crypto/rand, secrets, or SecureRandom for generating tokens, session IDs, salt, and nonces. Never use default PRNGs. Ensure compliant design across all execution branches.
why_is_this_important: Standard pseudo-random generators (such as math/rand or Math.random) are deterministic and predictable, allowing attackers to anticipate generated tokens and bypass authentication.

title: Prevent Command Injection by Avoiding Shell Execution (Standard Policy #23)
rule: Invoke executables directly by passing arguments as discrete array elements rather than executing commands through an interactive shell (/bin/sh -c). Never interpolate untrusted strings into system commands. Ensure compliant design across all execution branches.
why_is_this_important: Shell command injection (CWE-78) allows remote adversaries to execute unauthorized operating system commands with the privileges of the application process.

title: Prevent Path Traversal by Validating and Sanitizing File Paths (Standard Policy #23)
rule: Resolve canonical file paths using secure path resolution APIs and verify that target paths remain strictly confined within an authorized root directory before performing file I/O operations. Ensure compliant design across all execution branches.
why_is_this_important: Path traversal vulnerabilities (CWE-22) allow attackers to access arbitrary files on the filesystem, including sensitive system configurations and credentials.
good_example: cleanPath := filepath.Clean(userInputPath); if !strings.HasPrefix(cleanPath, rootDir) { return ErrForbidden }

examples.snippet: cleanPath := filepath.Clean(userInputPath); if !strings.HasPrefix(cleanPath, rootDir) { return ErrForbidden }

title: Prohibit Deprecated and Broken Cryptographic Hash Algorithms (Standard Policy #24)
rule: Avoid legacy hashing algorithms such as MD5 and SHA-1 for digital signatures, password verification, or integrity validation. Mandate modern primitives like SHA-256, SHA-3, or BLAKE3. Ensure compliant design across all execution branches.
why_is_this_important: MD5 and SHA-1 suffer from proven practical collision attacks, rendering them unsuitable for security verification and digital signatures.

title: Enforce Password Hashing using Argon2id or Bcrypt (Standard Policy #24)
rule: Store user passwords using slow, memory-hard hashing algorithms such as Argon2id or Bcrypt with an appropriate cost factor. Never store plaintext, salted SHA-256, or fast hashes. Ensure compliant design across all execution branches.
why_is_this_important: Fast hash algorithms allow high-throughput GPU/ASIC offline dictionary attacks, exposing user credentials in the event of database exfiltration.

title: Avoid Hardcoded Cryptographic Keys and Shared Secrets (Standard Policy #24)
rule: Never embed symmetric encryption keys, HMAC secrets, or private certificates directly into source code. Inject them at runtime via secure environment managers or KMS envelopes. Ensure compliant design across all execution branches.
why_is_this_important: Hardcoded secrets in source code persist in version control history and decompiled binaries, leading to total compromise of cryptographic protections.

title: Verify Inbound Webhook Signatures using Constant-Time Comparison (Standard Policy #24)
rule: Always verify cryptographic HMAC signatures on incoming webhook payloads before parsing or processing. Use constant-time comparison algorithms to mitigate timing attacks. Ensure compliant design across all execution branches.
why_is_this_important: Accepting unverified webhook payloads allows malicious third parties to spoof events, manipulate balances, and trigger unauthorized automated actions.

title: Enforce Strict CORS Origin Whitelisting (Standard Policy #24)
rule: Configure Cross-Origin Resource Sharing (CORS) with an explicit whitelist of trusted origins. Never combine Access-Control-Allow-Origin: * with credentials enabled. Ensure compliant design across all execution branches.
why_is_this_important: Wildcard CORS combined with credentials allows malicious third-party websites to make authenticated cross-origin requests on behalf of logged-in users.

title: Prevent XML External Entity (XXE) Injection (Standard Policy #24)
rule: Disable external entity resolution (DTD) and entity expansion when parsing untrusted XML payloads in any parser or processor. Ensure compliant design across all execution branches.
why_is_this_important: XXE injection (CWE-611) allows attackers to read arbitrary server files, conduct internal port scans, or cause denial-of-service.

title: Prevent Server-Side Request Forgery (SSRF) on Outbound Requests (Standard Policy #24)
rule: Validate, sanitize, and restrict target destination URLs for outbound HTTP requests against an explicit domain allowlist and private IP filter (prevent access to RFC 1918 and link-local ranges). Ensure compliant design across all execution branches.
why_is_this_important: SSRF vulnerabilities (CWE-918) permit attackers to interact with internal cloud metadata services, VPC resources, and unauthenticated internal daemons.

title: Prevent Unbounded Goroutine or Thread Spawning (Standard Policy #24)
rule: Always dispatch asynchronous tasks through bounded worker pools or rate-limited semaphores. Never spawn bare goroutines or detached threads directly in request handlers. Ensure compliant design across all execution branches.
why_is_this_important: Unbounded thread/goroutine allocation under traffic spikes exhausts memory and scheduling resources, causing process crashes and denial of service.

title: Protect Concurrent Map Access with Mutual Exclusion (Standard Policy #24)
rule: Synchronize shared map reads and writes using sync.RWMutex, ConcurrentHashMap, or thread-safe sync.Map primitives. Ensure compliant design across all execution branches.
why_is_this_important: Concurrent unsynchronized reads and writes on native maps trigger fatal runtime panics and corrupt application state.

title: Mandate Resource Cleanup via Defer or Try-With-Resources (Standard Policy #24)
rule: Ensure all acquired I/O handles, file descriptors, database transactions, and network connections are guaranteed to be closed using defer, using/try-with-resources statements. Ensure compliant design across all execution branches.
why_is_this_important: Failing to close resources on early return or error paths leaks file descriptors and socket pools, eventually halting process I/O.
good_example: file, err := os.Open(filename); if err != nil { return err }; defer file.Close()

examples.snippet: file, err := os.Open(filename); if err != nil { return err }; defer file.Close()

title: Enforce Context Cancellation and Propagation Across Asynchronous Calls (Standard Policy #24)
rule: Propagate context.Context across all outbound RPCs, database queries, and async routines. Respect ctx.Done() to terminate in-flight work when requests are canceled. Ensure compliant design across all execution branches.
why_is_this_important: Ignoring context cancellation results in orphaned background computations, resource waste, and server memory starvation.

title: Avoid Deadlock Hazards by Establishing Deterministic Lock Ordering (Standard Policy #24)
rule: When acquiring multiple mutual exclusion locks simultaneously, always acquire and release them in a consistent, globally deterministic order across all call paths. Ensure compliant design across all execution branches.
why_is_this_important: Inconsistent lock ordering across concurrent threads creates circular wait conditions, precipitating catastrophic application deadlocks.
bad_example: muB.Lock(); muA.Lock(); defer muA.Unlock(); defer muB.Unlock()
good_example: muA.Lock(); muB.Lock(); defer muB.Unlock(); defer muA.Unlock()

examples.snippet: muB.Lock(); muA.Lock(); defer muA.Unlock(); defer muB.Unlock()
muA.Lock(); muB.Lock(); defer muB.Unlock(); defer muA.Unlock()

title: Avoid Double-Closing Channels in Go (Standard Policy #24)
rule: Ensure a channel is only closed by the single designated sender goroutine that owns it. Never close a channel from multiple concurrent receiver routines. Ensure compliant design across all execution branches.
why_is_this_important: Closing an already closed channel causes an immediate, non-recoverable runtime panic in Go.

title: Prevent Unbuffered Channel Leaks on Early Exit (Standard Policy #24)
rule: Ensure sending to an unbuffered channel cannot block indefinitely if the receiving goroutine exits early due to errors or timeouts. Ensure compliant design across all execution branches.
why_is_this_important: Blocked goroutines waiting to send on unbuffered channels remain pinned in memory indefinitely, causing silent goroutine leaks.
bad_example: ch := make(chan int); go func() { ch <- compute() }()
good_example: ch := make(chan int, 1); go func() { ch <- compute() }(); return <-ch

examples.snippet: ch := make(chan int); go func() { ch <- compute() }()
ch := make(chan int, 1); go func() { ch <- compute() }(); return <-ch

title: Eliminate N+1 Query Antipattern in Data Fetching (Standard Policy #24)
rule: Eagerly load related relational records using batch queries (IN clauses, JOINs, or DataLoader patterns) instead of issuing individual queries inside iteration loops. Ensure compliant design across all execution branches.
why_is_this_important: Executing individual database round-trips inside loops causes significant query latency and database connection exhaustion under scale.

title: Enforce Pagination and Result Limits on Collection Endpoints (Standard Policy #24)
rule: Always enforce mandatory pagination limits (e.g. limit and offset or cursor tokens) on database queries returning collections. Never perform unbounded SELECT operations. Ensure compliant design across all execution branches.
why_is_this_important: Unbounded database queries can pull hundreds of thousands of records into memory, triggering out-of-memory crashes and saturating database I/O.
good_example: db.Query('SELECT * FROM audit_logs ORDER BY created_at DESC LIMIT $1 OFFSET $2', limit, offset)

examples.snippet: db.Query('SELECT * FROM audit_logs ORDER BY created_at DESC LIMIT $1 OFFSET $2', limit, offset)

title: Ensure Database Transactions Always Execute Rollback on Failure (Standard Policy #24)
rule: Always wrap database transaction scopes with deferred rollback guards to ensure failed operations clean up transaction locks and prevent dangling transactions. Ensure compliant design across all execution branches.
why_is_this_important: Uncommitted transactions left open due to early returns or runtime errors hold database locks and deplete transaction slots.
good_example: tx, err := db.Begin(); if err != nil { return err }; defer tx.Rollback(); doWork(tx); return tx.Commit()

examples.snippet: tx, err := db.Begin(); if err != nil { return err }; defer tx.Rollback(); doWork(tx); return tx.Commit()

title: Avoid Index Suppression by Applying Functions to Filter Columns (Standard Policy #24)
rule: Do not wrap indexed database columns in scalar functions within WHERE clauses (e.g., LOWER(email) or DATE(created_at)). Use functional indexes or range bounds instead. Ensure compliant design across all execution branches.
why_is_this_important: Applying functions to indexed columns invalidates index lookups, forcing the database engine to perform expensive full table scans.

title: Prohibit Swallowing Errors Without Logging or Propagation (Standard Policy #24)
rule: Always handle or propagate errors returned from fallible operations. Never discard errors with blank identifiers or empty catch blocks without explicit justification. Ensure compliant design across all execution branches.
why_is_this_important: Swallowing errors hides failures, causes silent state corruption, and turns production defects into impossible-to-diagnose phantom bugs.
good_example: data, err := os.ReadFile(path); if err != nil { return fmt.Errorf('read config: %w', err) }

examples.snippet: data, err := os.ReadFile(path); if err != nil { return fmt.Errorf('read config: %w', err) }

title: Enforce Structured Logging with Key-Value Context (Standard Policy #24)
rule: Emit log statements with structured key-value attributes (e.g., slog, zap, winston) rather than unparsed string formatting. Include correlation IDs and tenant identifiers. Ensure compliant design across all execution branches.
why_is_this_important: Unstructured string logs cannot be indexed, queried, or alerted upon reliably by modern log management platforms like Datadog, ELK, or OpenTelemetry.

title: Avoid Logging Sensitive Credentials or PII (Standard Policy #24)
rule: Sanitize and redact authorization headers, passwords, session tokens, social security numbers, and payment details before emitting log entries. Ensure compliant design across all execution branches.
why_is_this_important: Sensitive data in log streams frequently ends up in monitoring dashboards, third-party log providers, and developer laptops, violating privacy regulations.

title: Wrap Errors with Domain Context Rather Than Raw String Errors (Standard Policy #24)
rule: Wrap errors using standard formatters (%w in Go, custom error hierarchies in TypeScript/Python) to preserve underlying error causes while adding operation context. Ensure compliant design across all execution branches.
why_is_this_important: Returning bare error strings destroys stack traces and root cause inspectability, hindering effective automated error handling.

why_is_this_important: Standard pseudo-random generators (such as math/rand or Math.random) are deterministic and predictable, allowing attackers to anticipate generated tokens and bypass authentication.

title: Prevent Command Injection by Avoiding Shell Execution (Standard Policy #28)
rule: Invoke executables directly by passing arguments as discrete array elements rather than executing commands through an interactive shell (/bin/sh -c). Never interpolate untrusted strings into system commands. Ensure compliant design across all execution branches.
why_is_this_important: Shell command injection (CWE-78) allows remote adversaries to execute unauthorized operating system commands with the privileges of the application process.

title: Prevent Path Traversal by Validating and Sanitizing File Paths (Standard Policy #28)
rule: Resolve canonical file paths using secure path resolution APIs and verify that target paths remain strictly confined within an authorized root directory before performing file I/O operations. Ensure compliant design across all execution branches.
why_is_this_important: Path traversal vulnerabilities (CWE-22) allow attackers to access arbitrary files on the filesystem, including sensitive system configurations and credentials.
good_example: cleanPath := filepath.Clean(userInputPath); if !strings.HasPrefix(cleanPath, rootDir) { return ErrForbidden }

examples.snippet: cleanPath := filepath.Clean(userInputPath); if !strings.HasPrefix(cleanPath, rootDir) { return ErrForbidden }

title: Prohibit Deprecated and Broken Cryptographic Hash Algorithms (Standard Policy #28)
rule: Avoid legacy hashing algorithms such as MD5 and SHA-1 for digital signatures, password verification, or integrity validation. Mandate modern primitives like SHA-256, SHA-3, or BLAKE3. Ensure compliant design across all execution branches.
why_is_this_important: MD5 and SHA-1 suffer from proven practical collision attacks, rendering them unsuitable for security verification and digital signatures.

title: Enforce Password Hashing using Argon2id or Bcrypt (Standard Policy #28)
rule: Store user passwords using slow, memory-hard hashing algorithms such as Argon2id or Bcrypt with an appropriate cost factor. Never store plaintext, salted SHA-256, or fast hashes. Ensure compliant design across all execution branches.
why_is_this_important: Fast hash algorithms allow high-throughput GPU/ASIC offline dictionary attacks, exposing user credentials in the event of database exfiltration.

title: Avoid Hardcoded Cryptographic Keys and Shared Secrets (Standard Policy #28)
rule: Never embed symmetric encryption keys, HMAC secrets, or private certificates directly into source code. Inject them at runtime via secure environment managers or KMS envelopes. Ensure compliant design across all execution branches.
why_is_this_important: Hardcoded secrets in source code persist in version control history and decompiled binaries, leading to total compromise of cryptographic protections.

title: Verify Inbound Webhook Signatures using Constant-Time Comparison (Standard Policy #28)
rule: Always verify cryptographic HMAC signatures on incoming webhook payloads before parsing or processing. Use constant-time comparison algorithms to mitigate timing attacks. Ensure compliant design across all execution branches.
why_is_this_important: Accepting unverified webhook payloads allows malicious third parties to spoof events, manipulate balances, and trigger unauthorized automated actions.

title: Enforce Strict CORS Origin Whitelisting (Standard Policy #28)
rule: Configure Cross-Origin Resource Sharing (CORS) with an explicit whitelist of trusted origins. Never combine Access-Control-Allow-Origin: * with credentials enabled. Ensure compliant design across all execution branches.
why_is_this_important: Wildcard CORS combined with credentials allows malicious third-party websites to make authenticated cross-origin requests on behalf of logged-in users.

title: Prevent XML External Entity (XXE) Injection (Standard Policy #29)
rule: Disable external entity resolution (DTD) and entity expansion when parsing untrusted XML payloads in any parser or processor. Ensure compliant design across all execution branches.
why_is_this_important: XXE injection (CWE-611) allows attackers to read arbitrary server files, conduct internal port scans, or cause denial-of-service.

title: Prevent Server-Side Request Forgery (SSRF) on Outbound Requests (Standard Policy #29)
rule: Validate, sanitize, and restrict target destination URLs for outbound HTTP requests against an explicit domain allowlist and private IP filter (prevent access to RFC 1918 and link-local ranges). Ensure compliant design across all execution branches.
why_is_this_important: SSRF vulnerabilities (CWE-918) permit attackers to interact with internal cloud metadata services, VPC resources, and unauthenticated internal daemons.

title: Prevent Unbounded Goroutine or Thread Spawning (Standard Policy #29)
rule: Always dispatch asynchronous tasks through bounded worker pools or rate-limited semaphores. Never spawn bare goroutines or detached threads directly in request handlers. Ensure compliant design across all execution branches.
why_is_this_important: Unbounded thread/goroutine allocation under traffic spikes exhausts memory and scheduling resources, causing process crashes and denial of service.

title: Protect Concurrent Map Access with Mutual Exclusion (Standard Policy #29)
rule: Synchronize shared map reads and writes using sync.RWMutex, ConcurrentHashMap, or thread-safe sync.Map primitives. Ensure compliant design across all execution branches.
why_is_this_important: Concurrent unsynchronized reads and writes on native maps trigger fatal runtime panics and corrupt application state.

title: Mandate Resource Cleanup via Defer or Try-With-Resources (Standard Policy #29)
rule: Ensure all acquired I/O handles, file descriptors, database transactions, and network connections are guaranteed to be closed using defer, using/try-with-resources statements. Ensure compliant design across all execution branches.
why_is_this_important: Failing to close resources on early return or error paths leaks file descriptors and socket pools, eventually halting process I/O.
good_example: file, err := os.Open(filename); if err != nil { return err }; defer file.Close()

examples.snippet: file, err := os.Open(filename); if err != nil { return err }; defer file.Close()

title: Enforce Context Cancellation and Propagation Across Asynchronous Calls (Standard Policy #29)
rule: Propagate context.Context across all outbound RPCs, database queries, and async routines. Respect ctx.Done() to terminate in-flight work when requests are canceled. Ensure compliant design across all execution branches.
why_is_this_important: Ignoring context cancellation results in orphaned background computations, resource waste, and server memory starvation.

title: Avoid Deadlock Hazards by Establishing Deterministic Lock Ordering (Standard Policy #29)
rule: When acquiring multiple mutual exclusion locks simultaneously, always acquire and release them in a consistent, globally deterministic order across all call paths. Ensure compliant design across all execution branches.
why_is_this_important: Inconsistent lock ordering across concurrent threads creates circular wait conditions, precipitating catastrophic application deadlocks.
bad_example: muB.Lock(); muA.Lock(); defer muA.Unlock(); defer muB.Unlock()
good_example: muA.Lock(); muB.Lock(); defer muB.Unlock(); defer muA.Unlock()

examples.snippet: muB.Lock(); muA.Lock(); defer muA.Unlock(); defer muB.Unlock()
muA.Lock(); muB.Lock(); defer muB.Unlock(); defer muA.Unlock()

title: Avoid Double-Closing Channels in Go (Standard Policy #29)
rule: Ensure a channel is only closed by the single designated sender goroutine that owns it. Never close a channel from multiple concurrent receiver routines. Ensure compliant design across all execution branches.
why_is_this_important: Closing an already closed channel causes an immediate, non-recoverable runtime panic in Go.

title: Prevent Unbuffered Channel Leaks on Early Exit (Standard Policy #29)
rule: Ensure sending to an unbuffered channel cannot block indefinitely if the receiving goroutine exits early due to errors or timeouts. Ensure compliant design across all execution branches.
why_is_this_important: Blocked goroutines waiting to send on unbuffered channels remain pinned in memory indefinitely, causing silent goroutine leaks.
bad_example: ch := make(chan int); go func() { ch <- compute() }()
good_example: ch := make(chan int, 1); go func() { ch <- compute() }(); return <-ch

examples.snippet: ch := make(chan int); go func() { ch <- compute() }()
ch := make(chan int, 1); go func() { ch <- compute() }(); return <-ch

title: Eliminate N+1 Query Antipattern in Data Fetching (Standard Policy #29)
rule: Eagerly load related relational records using batch queries (IN clauses, JOINs, or DataLoader patterns) instead of issuing individual queries inside iteration loops. Ensure compliant design across all execution branches.
why_is_this_important: Executing individual database round-trips inside loops causes significant query latency and database connection exhaustion under scale.

title: Enforce Pagination and Result Limits on Collection Endpoints (Standard Policy #29)
rule: Always enforce mandatory pagination limits (e.g. limit and offset or cursor tokens) on database queries returning collections. Never perform unbounded SELECT operations. Ensure compliant design across all execution branches.
why_is_this_important: Unbounded database queries can pull hundreds of thousands of records into memory, triggering out-of-memory crashes and saturating database I/O.
good_example: db.Query('SELECT * FROM audit_logs ORDER BY created_at DESC LIMIT $1 OFFSET $2', limit, offset)

examples.snippet: db.Query('SELECT * FROM audit_logs ORDER BY created_at DESC LIMIT $1 OFFSET $2', limit, offset)

title: Ensure Database Transactions Always Execute Rollback on Failure (Standard Policy #29)
rule: Always wrap database transaction scopes with deferred rollback guards to ensure failed operations clean up transaction locks and prevent dangling transactions. Ensure compliant design across all execution branches.
why_is_this_important: Uncommitted transactions left open due to early returns or runtime errors hold database locks and deplete transaction slots.
good_example: tx, err := db.Begin(); if err != nil { return err }; defer tx.Rollback(); doWork(tx); return tx.Commit()

examples.snippet: tx, err := db.Begin(); if err != nil { return err }; defer tx.Rollback(); doWork(tx); return tx.Commit()

title: Avoid Index Suppression by Applying Functions to Filter Columns (Standard Policy #29)
rule: Do not wrap indexed database columns in scalar functions within WHERE clauses (e.g., LOWER(email) or DATE(created_at)). Use functional indexes or range bounds instead. Ensure compliant design across all execution branches.
why_is_this_important: Applying functions to indexed columns invalidates index lookups, forcing the database engine to perform expensive full table scans.

title: Prohibit Swallowing Errors Without Logging or Propagation (Standard Policy #29)
rule: Always handle or propagate errors returned from fallible operations. Never discard errors with blank identifiers or empty catch blocks without explicit justification. Ensure compliant design across all execution branches.
why_is_this_important: Swallowing errors hides failures, causes silent state corruption, and turns production defects into impossible-to-diagnose phantom bugs.
good_example: data, err := os.ReadFile(path); if err != nil { return fmt.Errorf('read config: %w', err) }

examples.snippet: data, err := os.ReadFile(path); if err != nil { return fmt.Errorf('read config: %w', err) }

title: Enforce Structured Logging with Key-Value Context (Standard Policy #29)
rule: Emit log statements with structured key-value attributes (e.g., slog, zap, winston) rather than unparsed string formatting. Include correlation IDs and tenant identifiers. Ensure compliant design across all execution branches.
why_is_this_important: Unstructured string logs cannot be indexed, queried, or alerted upon reliably by modern log management platforms like Datadog, ELK, or OpenTelemetry.

title: Avoid Logging Sensitive Credentials or PII (Standard Policy #29)
rule: Sanitize and redact authorization headers, passwords, session tokens, social security numbers, and payment details before emitting log entries. Ensure compliant design across all execution branches.
why_is_this_important: Sensitive data in log streams frequently ends up in monitoring dashboards, third-party log providers, and developer laptops, violating privacy regulations.

title: Wrap Errors with Domain Context Rather Than Raw String Errors (Standard Policy #29)
rule: Wrap errors using standard formatters (%w in Go, custom error hierarchies in TypeScript/Python) to preserve underlying error causes while adding operation context. Ensure compliant design across all execution branches.
why_is_this_important: Returning bare error strings destroys stack traces and root cause inspectability, hindering effective automated error handling.

title: Enforce Proper HTTP Status Code Semantics (Standard Policy #29)
rule: Return semantically appropriate HTTP status codes (200 for OK, 201 for Created, 400 for Client Error, 401 for Unauthenticated, 403 for Forbidden, 404 for Not Found). Never return 200 with an error payload. Ensure compliant design across all execution branches.
why_is_this_important: Returning HTTP 200 with embedded error flags breaks HTTP caching layers, API gateways, monitoring alerts, and client retry logic.

title: Implement Distributed Idempotency on State-Mutating Endpoints (Standard Policy #29)
rule: Ensure billing, payment, and critical resource creation endpoints require and enforce unique idempotency keys to prevent duplicate execution on network retries. Ensure compliant design across all execution branches.
why_is_this_important: Transient network retries without idempotency keys lead to double charges, duplicate records, and inconsistent external system states.
good_example: func CreatePayment(w http.ResponseWriter, r *http.Request) { key := r.Header.Get('Idempotency-Key'); dedupeAndExecute(key) }

examples.snippet: func CreatePayment(w http.ResponseWriter, r *http.Request) { key := r.Header.Get('Idempotency-Key'); dedupeAndExecute(key) }

title: Maintain API Versioning and Prevent Breaking Changes (Standard Policy #29)
rule: Introduce new API fields as optional additions and maintain existing endpoint schemas under versioned prefixes (/v1, /v2) to ensure backward compatibility for mobile and third-party clients. Ensure compliant design across all execution branches.
why_is_this_important: Renaming or removing fields in unversioned API contracts instantly crashes older mobile app releases and third-party integrations.

title: Prevent SQL Injection via Parameterized Queries (Standard Policy #29)
rule: Always use parameterized queries, prepared statements, or ORM bound variables when constructing database queries. Never concatenate untrusted user input directly into SQL strings. Ensure compliant design across all execution branches.
why_is_this_important: Unsanitized string concatenation in queries exposes the database to severe SQL injection vulnerabilities (CWE-89), potentially resulting in unauthorized data exfiltration or table destruction.
bad_example: db.Query('SELECT * FROM users WHERE email = ' + email)
good_example: db.Query('SELECT * FROM users WHERE email = $1', email)

examples.snippet: db.Query('SELECT * FROM users WHERE email = ' + email)
db.Query('SELECT * FROM users WHERE email = $1', email)

rule: Encode or sanitize all user-supplied content before rendering it into HTML, DOM attributes, or JavaScript execution contexts. Avoid raw innerHTML or unescaped template bindings. Ensure compliant design across all execution branches.
why_is_this_important: Unescaped user input rendered into the DOM enables attackers to execute arbitrary scripts in user sessions (CWE-79), compromising authentication tokens and private user data.
